title: A pact
hookLine: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other

cards: Two hikers reach a fork in a trail at dusk and agree to split up. Whoever finds the way down first comes back for the other. It's a simple deal, and it only works if both of them would really come back.
Upatissa and Kolita make a deal like that, not about a trail, but about the deepest thing they can name. They've left the festival and their families' comforts to live as wanderers.
And along the way they make each other a promise that will shape the rest of their lives.

teach.h: A TEACHER WITH NO MORE TO GIVE.
teach.b: First, the teacher. In Rajagaha lives a wandering teacher named Sanjaya, with a large following of wanderers. The two friends go forth under him.
The commentaries say they quickly learned everything he had to teach, and then asked: is there more? There wasn't.

In another discourse, Sanjaya is remembered for answers that slip away when you reach for them: asked a hard question, he would say neither yes, nor no, nor neither. For these two, that was not a place to stop.
Second, the word. What were they looking for?
The Vinaya uses one word for it: the deathless. In Pali, amata. Not long life.
Not a heaven that might end. The deathless names freedom from the whole round of birth and death, the thing the festival couldn't give. Third, the pact.

teach.h: WHOEVER FINDS IT FIRST WILL TELL.
teach.b: As the Vinaya tells it, the two had given their word to each other: whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other. No conditions. No race.
No prize for winning. Just: if I get there, you'll hear of it. Fourth, why it matters.
A seeker could easily turn inward and forget everyone else.
These two built friendship into the search itself; each one's freedom was tied to the other's.

And the pact assumes something: that one of them might get there without the other, and that whoever did would not be too proud, too busy or too far gone to come back. Tomorrow, one of them finds something.

how: Buddhist teaching gives great weight to good friendship; in the discourses the Buddha calls admirable friendship the whole of the holy life (SN 45.2), and in some communities monks and lay people practice in small groups who support each other.

o: a vow never to go back to their families
a contract to serve one teacher for life
a promise the two friends make to each other

p: whoever finds it first will tell

s: the friends found what they were looking for with Sanjaya
they learned all he had, asked for more, and there wasn't any.
'the deathless' here means living a very long life
it names freedom from the whole round of birth and death.
the pact said whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other
no race, no prize: if one gets there, the other will hear.

games.q: you and your best friend are both searching for the same freedom. you might find it apart. what do you agree?
o: each of us keeps whatever we find.
whoever finds it first tells the other.
we stop searching until we can go together.
games.why: the Vinaya says they gave their word: whoever reaches the deathless first will tell the other.

practice: Bring a friend to mind, someone whose good you want, and think of one small, honest promise you could keep for them: not a grand vow, just something true. Hold it, picture keeping it, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: A pact. Two friends, wanderers under Sanjaya, promise each other: whoever finds the deathless first will tell the other. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali amata, the deathless (Sanskrit amrita), a name for nibbana.

carryVoice: Your line: whoever finds it first. Friendship, built into the search itself. See you tomorrow.
